A.explanation: This is the lost volts across the $0.1 \, \Omega$ internal resistance, $Ir$, not the terminal p.d. across the $2.0 \, \Omega$ resistor.

B.explanation: The current is about $2.86 \, \text{A}$ and the terminal p.d. is $E - Ir = 6.0 - 0.29 = 5.7 \, \text{V}$, which is also the p.d. across the $2.0 \, \Omega$ resistor.

C.explanation: This is the e.m.f. of $6.0 \, \text{V}$ and ignores the $0.3 \, \text{V}$ drop across the $0.1 \, \Omega$ internal resistance when current flows.

D.explanation: This incorrectly adds the internal drop to the e.m.f. as $E + Ir$, whereas the terminal p.d. is $E - Ir$ when the cell supplies current.

hints: Notice the voltmeter is connected across the $2.0 \, \Omega$ resistor, which is also the terminal p.d. of the $6.0 \, \text{V}$ source with $0.1 \, \Omega$ in series.
Recall that current in this single loop is limited by total resistance $0.1 + 2.0 = 2.1 \, \Omega$, so use $I = E / R_{total}$.
Then find the voltmeter reading either as $V = I \times 2.0 \, \Omega$ or as $V = E - I \times 0.1 \, \Omega$.
walkthrough: Identify the loop: e.m.f. $E = 6.0 \, \text{V}$ drives current through internal resistance $r = 0.1 \, \Omega$ and external resistance $R = 2.0 \, \Omega$ in series.
Find the current using $I = E / (R + r)$. So $I = 6.0 / (2.0 + 0.1) = 6.0 / 2.1 \approx 2.86 \, \text{A}$.
The voltmeter reads the p.d. across the $2.0 \, \Omega$ resistor: $V = IR = 2.86 \times 2.0 \approx 5.71 \, \text{V}$.
Check with lost volts: $Ir \approx 2.86 \times 0.1 \approx 0.29 \, \text{V}$, so terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir \approx 6.0 - 0.29 = 5.71 \, \text{V}$.
Rounded to two significant figures this is $5.7 \, \text{V}$. This is option B.
